lesson.title: Gaining and losing electrons

lead.text: Think of an atom as a bank account with two kinds of entry. Each proton adds +1 and each electron adds −1. The charge of the atom is the balance when all the entries are in. A neutral atom is the case from the first lesson, where the entries cancel and the balance is zero.

The balance changes only when the number of electrons changes. If an atom takes on an extra electron or loses one, the entries no longer cancel. An atom that carries a charge in this way is called an ion. For an atom with p protons and e electrons, the charge is p − e.

afterFigure.text: Lithium shows the account being altered. A neutral lithium atom has 3 protons and 3 electrons, so its balance is 3 − 3 = 0. Remove one electron and 2 are left against the same 3 protons, so the balance becomes 3 − 2 = +1. The atom has become an ion, and the picture shows it beside the neutral atom.

lead.text: A sodium atom has lost one of its electrons. Treat each proton as +1 and each electron as −1, and work out the balance.

The sign of the balance depends on which side of the account is larger. An atom that loses electrons has more protons than electrons, so the positive entries win and the ion is positive. An atom that gains electrons has more electrons than protons, so the negative entries win and the ion is negative.

The size of the charge is the size of the gap. An ion that is two electrons short has a charge of +2, and one with four electrons too many has a charge of −4. Always write the sign, because −4 and +4 describe very different ions.

The same account tells you how many electrons an ion has. Start from the neutral atom, which has as many electrons as protons. With 7 protons it has 7 electrons, so after gaining 2 it has 9 and a charge of 7 − 9 = −2.

diagram.alt: A ledger for an atom with 7 protons. A row of plus signs for the protons sits above a row of minus signs for the electrons, joined in pairs. Unpaired signs are highlighted and decide the sign and size of the charge.
diagram.caption: Each plus is a proton and each minus an electron. Pairs cancel and the highlighted ones left over give the charge. Use the buttons to change the number of electrons.

lead.text: Follow the balance from a neutral atom to an ion. At the start the entries cancel, and then three electrons arrive.

steps.headline: Electrons move and the nucleus stays

lead.text: Something stays fixed through all of this accounting, and that is the protons. In ordinary chemistry only electrons move between atoms and the nucleus is left alone, so an atom that becomes an ion is still an atom of the same element.

A sodium atom and a sodium ion both have 11 protons, so both are sodium. The ion has a different number of electrons, so it has a different charge and it behaves differently. Sodium metal reacts violently with water, while sodium ions float quietly in seawater, even though the nucleus is the same in both.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the neutral atom and the ion side by side. Count the particles in each nucleus and then count the particles round it. The nucleus is the same in both, and the electron count is the only thing that differs.

steps.headline: Writing the charge of an ion

lead.text: Chemists have a short way of writing an ion. After the symbol of the element, they put the charge as a small raised number. The size comes first and the sign second, and a charge of 1 is written as the sign alone. A beryllium atom that has lost two electrons is Be²⁺, and a chlorine atom that has gained one is Cl⁻.
Read these the way the account would. Be²⁺ says the protons exceed the electrons by 2, and Cl⁻ says the electrons exceed the protons by 1. The examples that follow use the same bookkeeping.

afterFigure.text: Compare the two ions in the picture with their symbols. Beryllium has 4 protons and 2 electrons, so its charge is +2. Chlorine has 17 protons and 18 electrons, so its charge is −1. Notice that the sign is the same sign you get from p − e.

lead.text: Think about which entry in the account changes when an electron leaves, and which entry does not.

steps.headline: A magnesium ion has 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its charge?

workedSteps.text: There are more protons, so the positive charges win.

steps.headline: An oxide ion has 8 protons and 10 electrons. Find its charge.

workedSteps.text: Subtract the electrons from the protons.
Say what the charge is, with its sign.

lead.text: Aluminium commonly forms an ion by losing three electrons. Compare its protons with its electrons now.

blocks.text: Rub a balloon on your hair for a few seconds and then press it against a wall. It stays there. Hold it near a thin stream of water from a tap and the stream bends towards it. Nothing about the balloon looks different, yet it now pulls on things that it ignored before.

What changed is a handful of electrons. Rubbing moved some of them from your hair onto the balloon, so the balloon ended up with extra negative charge and your hair with a shortage. Both started with no overall charge. The last lesson showed that an atom's electrons can change while its nucleus stays the same, and this is an everyday case of it.

This lesson keeps an account for a single atom. We count the charges that come with its protons and its electrons, and watch the balance change as electrons leave or arrive. The balance tells us the charge the atom carries, and what we call it.

diagram.caption: Each plus is a positive charge and each minus a negative one. Rubbing moved two electrons from the hair to the balloon. Use the buttons to compare before and after.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out an ion's charge from its protons and electrons, and say what stays the same when an ion forms.
intro.whyItMatters: Ions are how atoms hand charge to one another, and that is the start of how compounds form.

recap.keyIdea: An ion's charge is its proton count minus its electron count. Losing electrons makes it positive and gaining them makes it negative, and the element never changes.

blocks.text: Back at the balloon, the electrons that moved from hair to rubber are the same kind of change. You found that 11 protons with 10 electrons give +1 and that 8 protons with 10 electrons give −2. Each time you took the electrons away from the protons and kept the sign.

recap.nextHook: Not all electrons are equally easy to move, because the ones on the outside of an atom are the ones that leave and arrive. The next lesson finds where an atom's electrons sit and which ones are on the outside.

questions.prompt: A sodium ion has 11 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: Count positive charges minus negative charges.
Use charge = proton count − electron count.
Calculate 11 − 10.
questions.onCorrect: +1. Eleven protons against ten electrons leaves one unit of positive charge.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two counts. Charge compares them.
The sign is the wrong way round. More protons than electrons gives a positive charge.

questions.prompt: An oxide ion has 8 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: More electrons than protons gives negative charge.
Subtract all ten negative charges from eight positive charges.
Calculate 8 − 10, keeping the sign.
questions.onCorrect: −2. Two more electrons than protons leaves two units of negative charge.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Ten electrons outnumber eight protons, so the charge is negative.
That adds the two counts. Charge compares them.

questions.prompt: What happens when a neutral atom loses one electron?
hints: Which entry in the account changes when an electron leaves?
The nucleus stays unchanged.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Removing a negative charge leaves a net positive charge.

questions.onCorrect: Losing a negative electron leaves a net positive charge, and the nucleus is untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: Electrons are negative. Taking one away makes the atom more positive.
Losing an electron does not touch the nucleus, so the atomic number stays.

questions.prompt: An aluminium ion has 13 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: Subtract electrons from protons.
There are three more protons than electrons.
Calculate 13 − 10.
questions.onCorrect: +3. Thirteen protons against ten electrons: three more positive than negative.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two counts. Charge compares them.
The sign is the wrong way round. More protons than electrons gives a positive charge.

questions.prompt: A fluoride ion has 9 protons and 10 electrons. Enter its signed charge.
hints: One extra electron contributes one negative charge.
Electrons outnumber protons by one.
Calculate 9 − 10, keeping the sign.
questions.onCorrect: −1. One more electron than protons leaves one unit of negative charge.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Electrons outnumber protons here, so the charge is negative.
That adds the two counts. Charge compares them.

questions.prompt: Mg²⁺ and a neutral magnesium atom share what?
hints: Identity follows the nucleus.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both have twelve protons; Mg²⁺ has two fewer electrons.

questions.onCorrect: Both have twelve protons. The ion has lost two electrons, but it is still magnesium.

misconceptions.feedback: The ion has lost two electrons, so the electron counts differ.
The ion is positive and the atom is neutral, so the charges differ.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom has 5 protons and 5 electrons. It then gains 3 more electrons. What is its charge now?
hints: Each electron carries a negative charge.
At first the five positive and five negative charges cancel. What changes after three more electrons?
Which kind of charge now has the larger count, and by how many?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 positive charges against 8 negative ones leaves 5 − 8 = −3.

questions.onCorrect: −3. Three extra electrons leave three units of negative charge. This is an ion, and its charge is protons minus electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Extra electrons make the atom negative.
That counts the electrons. Charge compares them with the protons.

questions.prompt: Why is the charge positive when there are more protons than electrons?

acceptedIdeas: Protons carry positive charge, so the surplus protons leave a net positive charge

choices.label: Protons carry positive charge, so the surplus protons leave a net positive charge
Electrons only count when the atom is neutral

questions.onCorrect: Right: charges cancel in pairs, and the unmatched protons are what remain.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass is not what sets charge. Each proton carries +1.
Electrons always count. Each one carries −1.

questions.prompt: A calcium ion has 20 protons and 18 electrons. What is its charge?
hints: Which is larger, the proton count or the electron count?
Subtract the electrons from the protons.
Keep the sign of the result.
questions.onCorrect: +2. More protons than electrons, by two, makes a 2+ ion.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. Protons outnumber electrons here.
That adds the two counts. Charge compares them.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom with 20 protons loses 2 electrons. How many electrons does the ion have?
hints: How many electrons does the neutral atom start with?
Neutral means electrons equal protons.
Take the lost electrons away from the starting count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Neutral: 20 electrons. After losing 2 there are 20 − 2 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Start from the neutral count and take away what was lost.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds electrons. The atom lost some.
That is the charge of the ion, not its electron count.
